The chapter builds from Bernoulli and multinomial variables to Gaussian distributions, mixtures, exponential-family models, and nonparametric methods. probability distributions maximum likelihood Bayesian inference Gaussian exponential family

The beta distribution acts as a conjugate prior for Bernoulli/binomial parameters, while the Dirichlet distribution plays the same role for multinomial probabilities. records.title: PRML Chapter 3 overview: linear models for regression
records.index_text: PRML Chapter 3 overview: linear models for regression Chapter 3 turns probabilistic modeling into supervised regression. It studies linear-in-the-parameters basis-function models, derives least squares from maximum likelihood, introduces regularization and the bias-variance tradeoff, then develops Bayesian linear regression through posterior weights, predictive distributions, equivalent kernels, model evidence, and evidence approximation. records.title: Linear basis functions and least squares
records.index_text: Linear basis functions and least squares The chapter begins with models that are linear in their weights but can be nonlinear in the input through basis functions. Maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise leads to least squares, and the geometric view explains fitting as projection onto the space spanned by basis functions. The section also covers sequential learning, regularized least squares, and multiple-output regression. Use this summary for questions about basis functions, least squares, and why linear models can represent nonlinear input transformations. basis function linear in parameters Gaussian noise least squares projection regularized least squares multiple outputs
records.display_text: The chapter begins with models that are linear in their weights but can be nonlinear in the input through basis functions. The section also covers sequential learning, regularized least squares, and multiple-output regression.

records.title: Bayesian regression, model comparison, and evidence
records.index_text: Bayesian regression, model comparison, and evidence The Bayesian part of Chapter 3 treats model weights as uncertain variables. A prior and likelihood produce a posterior over weights, and predictions integrate over that posterior. Model evidence supports comparison between models and hyperparameters; evidence approximation estimates regularization strength and the effective number of parameters. The chapter closes by noting limitations of fixed basis functions. Use this summary for questions about Bayesian regression, posterior prediction, model evidence, and why fixed basis functions can be limiting. records.title: Dense-X overview: retrieval granularity
records.index_text: Dense-X overview: retrieval granularity Dense-X Retrieval studies what unit should be indexed for dense retrieval. Instead of indexing only passages or sentences, the paper proposes propositions: atomic, self-contained, minimal factoids. The main claim is that retrieval quality depends heavily on granularity, and proposition-level indexing can reduce distractors while preserving precise evidence for question answering. Use this summary for questions about the Dense-X paper, proposition-level retrieval, or why retrieval unit size matters. dense retrieval retrieval granularity proposition factoid passage retrieval sentence retrieval open-domain question answering FactoidWiki
records.display_text: Dense-X Retrieval studies what unit should be indexed for dense retrieval. Instead of indexing only passages or sentences, the paper proposes propositions: atomic, self-contained, minimal factoids. The main claim is that retrieval quality depends heavily on granularity, and proposition-level indexing can reduce distractors while preserving precise evidence for question answering.

records.title: Proposition as a retrieval unit
records.index_text: Proposition as a retrieval unit A proposition is treated as a self-contained atomic expression that preserves one meaning. The paper positions propositions between sentences and passages: smaller than many sentences when a sentence has multiple facts, but more meaningful than arbitrary text fragments because the proposition keeps context needed for independent interpretation. Use this summary for questions asking what a proposition is, why a proposition differs from a sentence, or how proposition indexing helps retrieval. atomic fact self-contained meaning proposition sentence splitting passage splitting retrieval unit
records.display_text: A proposition is treated as a self-contained atomic expression that preserves one meaning. records.title: FactoidWiki and evaluation setup
records.index_text: FactoidWiki and evaluation setup The paper builds FactoidWiki by processing Wikipedia into different granularities such as passages, sentences, and propositions. It evaluates those index choices using open-domain QA datasets and dense retrievers, comparing whether finer-grained retrieval improves passage recall and downstream answer accuracy under a fixed retrieval budget. Use this summary for questions about the paper's dataset, evaluation method, and how it compares passage, sentence, and proposition indexes. FactoidWiki Wikipedia granularity comparison dense retriever open-domain QA retrieval budget passage recall

records.title: Dense-X results and lesson
records.index_text: Dense-X results and lesson The paper reports that proposition-level retrieval often improves retrieval and open-domain QA compared with coarser units. The practical lesson is that chunking is not just a preprocessing detail: index objects should match the granularity of user questions and preserve enough context to be independently useful. Use this summary for questions about what Dense-X found and how its findings apply to RAG chunking strategy. retrieval performance question answering fine-grained index context budget chunking strategy retrieval artifact
